sources.citation: Swanton, John R. 1940. Linguistic material from the tribes of Southern Texas and Northeastern Mexico. Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 127. Washington: GPO.
sources.note: Nothing about Aranama stress. The whole Aranama entry is 'WORDS IN ARANAMA: himia'na tsa'yi, give me water! / himiya'na, water.' (p. 124, p. 132). Phonetics pp. 9-10 say only 'The two Aranama words yield the following phonetics' [sound list] and, of accent marks, 'The accents in Comecrudo, Cotoname, and the Karankawa recorded by Dr. Gatschet are as given by the last named investigator' (p. 10) - no rule stated for any language, Aranama not mentioned there.

sources.citation: Swanton, John R. 1915. Linguistic position of the tribes of southern Texas and northeastern Mexico. American Anthropologist n.s. 17(1): 17-40.
sources.note: Nothing for Aranama. The paragraph gives an etymological parse of the two-word phrase (himiána ~ Coahuilteco awana 'water'; tsa- = 1sg objective prefix cf. Tonkawa ca, Coahuilteco tsin, Solano sa; -yi possibly 'give' cf. Comecrudo ayemá). The article's only use of 'stress' (p. 21) describes García's apostrophe in Coahuilteco ('the preceding consonant is pronounced with stress, i.e., like a fortis'), i.e. another language and not word stress. Accent marks on the Aranama forms are simply reproduced from Gatschet.

sources.citation: Gatschet, Albert S. 1886. Die Karánkawa-Indianer. Globus 49: 123-125. Braunschweig.
sources.note: Earliest printing of the two forms: 'Mein Tónkawe-Informant kannte zwei Wörter ihrer Sprache: himiyána, Wasser; himiána tsáyi! reiche mir Wasser!' (p. 124, right column). Acute accents on the penult of himiyána/himiána and on tsáyi; no statement about accent or stress.
